Chapter 9 Vibration of a system with one degree of freedom (nihanje sistema z eno prostostno stopnjo)

9.10 The convolution integral (konvolucijski integral)

In section 9.9 we saw that a short pulse (sunek) with impulse (impulz) \(I\) acts on the system roughly as the impulse response (impulzni odziv) \(I\,h(t)\) starts it. The cantilever with a mass (example A, mass \(m = 50\) kg, stiffness \(k = 62\,720\) N/m, damping ratio \(\zeta = 0{,}01\), natural period \(T_{\mathrm{n}} = 0{,}1774\) s) is not loaded by pulses only. The force on the mass may be given by a formula, or it may be measured by a force gauge, and then we know only its values at successive instants. The question of this section is whether the responses to short pieces of the force, each of which we can already compute, can be added, and what such a sum becomes when the pieces get ever shorter.

All the force acts on the same equation that we obtained in theorem 9.3,

\[m\,\ddot q + c\,\dot q + k\,q = Q(t) ,\]

where \(q\) is the generalized coordinate (generalizirana koordinata, for A the displacement of the end of the cantilever), \(Q(t)\) the generalized force on it, and \(c = 2\zeta\sqrt{km}\) the damping coefficient. At the start the system is at rest, \(q(0) = 0\) and \(\dot q(0) = 0\). An initial state that is not rest is included in theorem 9.79 as a free motion.

9.10.1 Adding the responses to pieces of the force

We cut the force \(Q(s)\) on the interval from \(0\) to \(t\) into strips (trakovi) of width \(\Delta s\), each with a point \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\) and the value of the force \(Q(s_{\mathrm{j}})\) there (figure 9.39, top). If \(\Delta s\) is much shorter than the natural period \(T_{\mathrm{n}}\), the strip acts as a pulse with impulse \(Q(s_{\mathrm{j}})\,\Delta s\) at time \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\), as in section 9.9. What is its response at a later time \(t\)? The impulse response \(h(t)\) (definition 9.74) is the response to the impulse \(1\) N s at time zero. The equation has constant coefficients, so if \(q(t)\) solves the equation with force \(Q(t)\), the function \(q(t - s)\) solves the equation with force \(Q(t - s)\): in differentiation with respect to \(t\) the shift \(s\) changes nothing, since the derivative of \(t \mapsto t - s\) is \(1\) (chain rule, lemma 8.29). The response from rest to a pulse at time \(s_{\mathrm{j}}\) is therefore \(h(t - s_{\mathrm{j}})\) for \(t \ge s_{\mathrm{j}}\), and before the pulse the system is at rest. Strip \(j\) contributes \(h(t - s_{\mathrm{j}})\,Q(s_{\mathrm{j}})\,\Delta s\). By lemma 9.6 the responses add, since the sum of solutions for forces \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) is a solution for \(Q_1 + Q_2\). The response at time \(t\) is therefore

\[q(t) \approx \sum_{\mathrm{s}_\mathrm{j} \le \mathrm{t}} h(t - s_{\mathrm{j}})\,Q(s_{\mathrm{j}})\,\Delta s ,\]

a sum that looks like a Riemann sum of the integral \(\int_0^t h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\).

Let us test this on A. We cut the force \(Q(s) = 20\ \text{N}\,\sin(\pi s/t_{\mathrm{p}})\) of duration \(t_{\mathrm{p}} = T_{\mathrm{n}}/2 = 0{,}0887\) s into \(6\) strips of width \(0{,}0148\) s and take the force at the midpoint of the strip. The sum at time \(t = 0{,}3\) s gives \(q = 0{,}16803\) mm. The integral \(\int_0^t h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\), which we computed with NumPy on \(4 \cdot 10^5\) division points, gives \(0{,}16793\) mm, so the sum agrees with the integral to \(0{,}06\) %. With \(2\), \(4\), \(8\) and \(16\) strips the deviation is \(+0{,}73\) %, \(+0{,}14\) %, \(+0{,}033\) % and \(+0{,}0082\) %: the strips get ever narrower and the sum approaches the integral.

This computation is an idea, not a proof. Each strip acts as a pulse only approximately (lemma 9.75 of section 9.9 gives the error for a rectangular pulse without damping), and to prove that the errors of all the strips do not accumulate we would have to estimate each of them separately. We therefore take another path. We write the formula \(\int_0^t h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\) as a candidate and check that it really solves the equation, and then uniqueness of the solution (theorem 9.36) shows that it is the only solution. The check requires differentiating an integral in which \(t\) appears both in the upper limit and in the integrand.

9.10.2 Derivative of an integral with upper limit \(t\)

What do we get if we differentiate \(G(t) = \int_0^t g(t, s)\,\mathrm{d}s\)? Lemma 4.19, point 2, covers exactly this form of limits for a continuous integrand, when the limits are \(\psi(t) = t\) and \(\varphi(t) = 0\). Its assumption is a continuous integrand, but the force \(Q(s)\) may be piecewise continuous (definition 6.8), for example a step or a rectangular pulse. We therefore split the interval into pieces on which \(Q\) is continuous and apply the lemma to each piece separately. The first term of the derivative is the value of the integrand at the upper limit, \(g(t, t)\,Q(t)\), the second is the integral of the derivative of the integrand with respect to \(t\), as if the limit were constant.

Lemma 9.77 Derivative of an integral whose upper limit is the parameter (odvod integrala, katerega zgornja meja je parameter)

Let \(T > 0\) and let \(g\) be a function with input the numbers \(t\) and \(s\) from the square \([0, T] \times [0, T]\) and output the number \(g(t, s)\). For every \(s \in [0, T]\) let the function \(t \mapsto g(t, s)\) be differentiable on \([0, T]\) (one-sided at the end points) with derivative \(\partial g/\partial t\), and let \(g\) and \(\partial g/\partial t\) be continuous on the square. Let \(Q\) be a piecewise continuous function on \([0, T]\) (definition 6.8) with partition \(0 = s_0 < s_1 < \dots < s_{\mathrm{r}} = T\) and functions \(Q_{\mathrm{i}}\) continuous on the closed pieces \([s_{\mathrm{i}}, s_{\mathrm{i}+1}]\). For \(t \in [0, T]\) let

\[G(t) = \int_0^t g(t, s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s .\]
  1. The function \(G\) is continuous on \([0, T]\).
  2. At every point \(t \in (0, T)\) that is not a break point, \(G\) is differentiable and
    \[G'(t) = g(t, t)\,Q(t) + \int_0^t \frac{\partial g}{\partial t}(t, s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s . \tag{9.70}\]
Proof

We have to show both points. The first follows from the uniform continuity of the kernel \(g\), the second from lemma 4.19 applied to the pieces on which \(Q\) is continuous. Here the integral of a piecewise continuous function has, by definition 6.9, the values of the functions \(Q_{\mathrm{i}}\) on the pieces, so we do not need the values of the force \(Q\) at the break points.

1. Continuity.

  1. The square is closed and bounded and \(g\) is continuous, so by theorem 1.78 there is \(M_{\mathrm{g}}\) with \(|g| \le M_{\mathrm{g}}\) on the square, and by theorem 4.6 \(g\) is uniformly continuous. Each of the functions \(Q_{\mathrm{i}}\) is continuous on a closed piece, so it is bounded by theorem 1.73. Let \(M_{\mathrm{Q}}\) be a number that is greater than or equal to \(|Q_{\mathrm{i}}|\) on \([s_{\mathrm{i}}, s_{\mathrm{i}+1}]\) for every \(i\).
  2. We choose \(\eta > 0\). By uniform continuity there is \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|g(t', s) - g(t, s)| < \eta/(2(T M_{\mathrm{Q}} + 1))\) for all \(s \in [0, T]\) and all \(t, t'\) with \(|t' - t| < \delta\). We decrease \(\delta\) so that also \(\delta \le \eta/(2(M_{\mathrm{g}} M_{\mathrm{Q}} + 1))\).
  3. Let \(0 \le t < t' \le T\) and \(t' - t < \delta\). We choose the partition of \([0, t']\) so that \(t\) is a break point. By independence of the integral of the partition and by linearity (lemma 6.10, points 1 and 2),
    \[G(t') - G(t) = \int_0^t \big(g(t', s) - g(t, s)\big)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s + \int_{\mathrm{t}}^{t'} g(t', s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s .\]
  4. If \(|f| \le B\) on \([a, b]\) for a piecewise continuous function \(f\), then \(|\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b f| \le B\,(b - a)\), because the functions \(B - f\) and \(B + f\) are nonnegative and their integral is nonnegative by points 2 and 3 of lemma 6.10. The first integral in step 3 is therefore in absolute value at most \(t \cdot \eta/(2(T M_{\mathrm{Q}} + 1)) \cdot M_{\mathrm{Q}} < \eta/2\), the second at most \((t' - t)\,M_{\mathrm{g}} M_{\mathrm{Q}} < \eta/2\).
  5. Hence \(|G(t') - G(t)| < \eta\). The same holds with \(t\) and \(t'\) exchanged, so \(G\) is continuous at every point of \([0, T]\).

2. Derivative.

  1. Let \(t \in (0, T)\) not be a break point, so \(s_{\mathrm{j}} < t < s_{\mathrm{j}+1}\) for some \(j\). For \(\tau \in (s_{\mathrm{j}}, s_{\mathrm{j}+1})\) equation (6.5) gives
    \[\begin{aligned} G(\tau) &= \sum_{\mathrm{i} < \mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{i}}(\tau) + B(\tau) , \\ A_{\mathrm{i}}(\tau) &= \int_{\mathrm{s}_\mathrm{i}}^{s_{\mathrm{i}+1}} g(\tau, s)\,Q_{\mathrm{i}}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s , \\ B(\tau) &= \int_{\mathrm{s}_\mathrm{j}}^{\tau} g(\tau, s)\,Q_{\mathrm{j}}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s . \end{aligned}\]
  2. In lemma 4.19 the integration variable is \(t\) and the parameter is \(s\). In our case the roles are exchanged, so we apply the lemma to the function \(f(s, \tau) = g(\tau, s)\,Q_{\mathrm{i}}(s)\) on the rectangle \([s_{\mathrm{i}}, s_{\mathrm{i}+1}] \times [s_{\mathrm{j}}, s_{\mathrm{j}+1}]\) (variable \(s\), parameter \(\tau\)). The function \(f\) is continuous as a product of continuous functions (corollary 1.64), for every \(s\) it is differentiable in \(\tau\) with derivative \(\partial g/\partial t(\tau, s)\,Q_{\mathrm{i}}(s)\), and this is continuous. Point 1 of the lemma gives for \(\tau = t \in (s_{\mathrm{j}}, s_{\mathrm{j}+1})\)
    \[A_{\mathrm{i}}'(t) = \int_{\mathrm{s}_\mathrm{i}}^{s_{\mathrm{i}+1}} \frac{\partial g}{\partial t}(t, s)\,Q_{\mathrm{i}}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s .\]
  3. The term \(B\) is an integral with limits \(\varphi(\tau) = s_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(\psi(\tau) = \tau\), for which \(s_{\mathrm{j}} \le \varphi \le \psi \le s_{\mathrm{j}+1}\) holds on \([s_{\mathrm{j}}, s_{\mathrm{j}+1}]\), with derivatives \(\varphi' = 0\) and \(\psi' = 1\). Point 2 of lemma 4.19, applied to the function \(f(s, \tau) = g(\tau, s)\,Q_{\mathrm{j}}(s)\) on the square \([s_{\mathrm{j}}, s_{\mathrm{j}+1}]^2\) (the assumptions are checked as in step 2), gives
    \[B'(t) = \int_{\mathrm{s}_\mathrm{j}}^{t} \frac{\partial g}{\partial t}(t, s)\,Q_{\mathrm{j}}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s + g(t, t)\,Q_{\mathrm{j}}(t) .\]
  4. Since \(t\) lies in an open piece, \(Q_{\mathrm{j}}(t) = Q(t)\). The derivative of a sum is the sum of derivatives, and the sum of the integrals over the pieces \([s_{\mathrm{i}}, s_{\mathrm{i}+1}]\) for \(i < j\) and over \([s_{\mathrm{j}}, t]\) is, by definition 6.9, the integral of the piecewise continuous function \(s \mapsto \partial g/\partial t(t, s)\,Q(s)\) over \([0, t]\). Hence \(G'(t)\) is the right-hand side of (9.70).

Source: The lemma is not from a source, as point 2 of lemma 4.19. For a continuous integrand it is the fundamental theorem of calculus with an upper limit (LEBL1, Theorem 5.3.3 and Remark 5.3.4, PDF pp. 202-203) and differentiation with respect to a parameter (LEBL2, Theorem 9.1.1, PDF pp. 65-66). The splitting into pieces because of the piecewise continuous force is ours.

The lemma showed that the upper limit \(t\) shows up in the derivative with two terms: with the integral of the derivative of the integrand, as if the limit were constant, and with the value of the integrand at the upper limit. For the kernel \(g(t, s) = h(t - s)\) this second term is \(h(0)\,Q(t) = 0\), because a pulse at time \(t\) has not yet moved the system by time \(t\).

9.10.3 Change of variable (zamenjava spremenljivke)

The integral of the response can be read in two ways. In \(\int_0^t h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\) the variable \(s\) is the time when the force acted and \(t - s\) is the time that has passed since then. In \(\int_0^t h(u)\,Q(t - u)\,\mathrm{d}u\) the variable \(u\) is the elapsed time and \(t - u\) is the time when the force acted. Both have the same value. Besides the reflection \(s \mapsto t - s\) we will need the shift \(s \mapsto s + d\), with which we move the start of the force to time zero. One lemma covers both substitutions, and we prove it by differentiating both sides.

Lemma 9.78 Change of variable in the integral (zamenjava spremenljivke v integralu)

Let \(G\) be a piecewise continuous function on \([p, q]\), \(p < q\), and \(d\) a real number. Then:

  1. (Reflection) \(\displaystyle\int_{\mathrm{d} - \mathrm{q}}^{d - p} G(d - v)\,\mathrm{d}v = \int_{\mathrm{p}}^q G(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  2. (Shift) \(\displaystyle\int_{\mathrm{p} - \mathrm{d}}^{q - d} G(v + d)\,\mathrm{d}v = \int_{\mathrm{p}}^q G(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\).

In particular, for piecewise continuous \(Q\) and continuous \(h\), every \(t\) and \(0 < \tau \le t\),

\[\begin{aligned} \int_0^t h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s &= \int_0^t h(u)\,Q(t - u)\,\mathrm{d}u , \\ \int_{\mathrm{t} - \tau}^{t} h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s &= \int_0^{\tau} h(u)\,Q(t - u)\,\mathrm{d}u . \end{aligned} \tag{9.71}\]
Proof

We have to show first both points for a continuous function on a closed interval, then for a piecewise continuous one piece by piece. The continuous case follows from the fundamental theorem of calculus, since the function \(F(\varphi(v))\) has derivative \(G(\varphi(v))\) up to a sign.

  1. Let \(G\) be continuous on \([p, q]\). With \(\sigma = -1\) we describe point 1 and with \(\sigma = 1\) point 2, so \(\varphi(v) = d + \sigma v\) maps the interval \(J\) from the left-hand side onto \([p, q]\). Let \(F(y) = \int_{\mathrm{p}}^y G(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\). By theorem 3.40, point 2, \(F\) is continuous on \([p, q]\) and \(F' = G\) there.
  2. Let \(K(v) = \sigma F(\varphi(v))\) on \(J\). The function \(K\) is continuous as a composition of continuous functions. The map \(\varphi\) takes the open interval \(J\) onto the open interval \((p, q)\), where \(F\) is continuously differentiable, and \(\varphi\) has derivative \(\sigma\). By the chain rule (lemma 8.29, point 1, for an interval) we have at every point \(v\) of the open interval \(K'(v) = \sigma\,F'(\varphi(v))\,\sigma = G(\varphi(v))\), because \(\sigma^2 = 1\). The function \(v \mapsto G(\varphi(v))\) is continuous on the closed \(J\).
  3. By theorem 3.40, point 1, \(\int_{\mathrm{J}} G(\varphi(v))\,\mathrm{d}v = K(\text{right end point}) - K(\text{left end point})\). For \(\sigma = -1\) the left end point is \(d - q\) with \(\varphi = q\) and the right one is \(d - p\) with \(\varphi = p\), so the difference is \(-F(p) + F(q)\). For \(\sigma = 1\) the left end point is \(p - d\) with \(\varphi = p\) and the right one is \(q - d\) with \(\varphi = q\), the difference is \(F(q) - F(p)\). In both cases this is \(F(q) = \int_{\mathrm{p}}^q G(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\), because \(F(p) = 0\).
  4. Let \(G\) be piecewise continuous with partition \(p = x_0 < \dots < x_{\mathrm{m}} = q\) and functions \(G_{\mathrm{k}}\). The function \(v \mapsto G(\varphi(v))\) is piecewise continuous with the partition obtained from the break points \(x_{\mathrm{k}}\) by the map \(\varphi^{-1}\) (for \(\sigma = -1\) in the reverse order). On the piece that corresponds to \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\) it equals the continuous function \(v \mapsto G_{\mathrm{k}}(\varphi(v))\). By step 3, applied to \(G_{\mathrm{k}}\) and the piece \([x_{\mathrm{k}-1}, x_{\mathrm{k}}]\), the integral of this function over the piece equals \(\int_{\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{k}-1}}^{x_{\mathrm{k}}} G_{\mathrm{k}}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\). We sum over \(k\) (definition 6.9).
  5. For the first equality in (9.71) we take point 1 with \(G(s) = h(t - s)\,Q(s)\), \(p = 0\), \(q = d = t\), since \(G(t - u) = h(u)\,Q(t - u)\). For the second equality we take point 1 with the same \(G\), \(p = t - \tau\), \(q = d = t\). The function \(G\) is piecewise continuous as a product of a continuous and a piecewise continuous function (corollary 1.64 on each piece).

Source: LEBL1, Theorem 5.3.5 (PDF p. 204), change of variable \(g(x) = d \pm x\) with the chain rule. The proof for this map, for piecewise continuous functions and for both points together is ours.

The lemma says that the roles of \(h\) and \(Q\) can be exchanged, as in a product of numbers. We use it for the periodic force later in the chapter, where \(Q(t - u)\) is the value of the force \(u\) seconds in the past. The second equality in (9.71), the integral from a start time \(t - \tau\), will be needed there when the start is not time zero.

9.10.4 Duhamel's theorem (Duhamelov izrek)

The check needs two agreements. The first is what a solution is when \(Q\) is piecewise continuous. We take the notion from section 9.4.4 for order \(2\): a solution on \([t_0, T]\) is a function \(q\) for which \(q\) and \(\dot q\) are continuous, \(\dot q\) is piecewise continuously differentiable (definition 6.11), and the equation holds at every point of the open interval \((t_0, T)\) that is not a break point of \(\dot q\) or of \(Q\). There \(\ddot q\) may have a jump. Theorem 9.36 is written for the start time \(0\). For the start time \(t_0\) it holds because the equation has no explicit time, as the last step of the proof below shows.

The second agreement is about the impulse response. The kernel \(h(t - s)\) must be defined on the whole square \([0, T]^2\), where \(t - s\) may be negative. The impulse response \(h\) of definition 9.74 is defined for every real argument and solves the free equation on the whole axis, so the kernel is defined everywhere. For negative arguments we do not care about the values, and the values \(h(t - s)\) for \(s > t\) do not enter the integral.

Theorem 9.79 Duhamel integral (Duhamelov integral)

Let \(m, k > 0\) and \(c \ge 0\) and let \(h\) be the impulse response (definition 9.74), which is defined for every real argument. Let \(t_0 < T\), \(Q\) a piecewise continuous function on \([t_0, T]\) and \(q_0, v_0\) real numbers. Let \(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) be solutions of the equation \(m\,\ddot\varphi + c\,\dot\varphi + k\,\varphi = 0\) with \(\varphi_1(0) = 1\), \(\dot\varphi_1(0) = 0\) and \(\varphi_2(0) = 0\), \(\dot\varphi_2(0) = 1\) (they exist by theorem 9.36) and let

\[q_{\mathrm{pr}}(t) = q_0\,\varphi_1(t - t_0) + v_0\,\varphi_2(t - t_0)\]

be the free motion (prosto gibanje) with the values \(q_0\) and \(v_0\) at time \(t_0\) (theorem 9.43). Then

\[q(t) = q_{\mathrm{pr}}(t) + \int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^t h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s \tag{9.72}\]

is the only solution on \([t_0, T]\) with \(q(t_0) = q_0\) and \(\dot q(t_0) = v_0\). The free part is linear in the pair \((q_0, v_0)\), the integral part does not depend on them. The solution \(q\) is continuously differentiable on \([t_0, T]\) and

\[\dot q(t) = \dot q_{\mathrm{pr}}(t) + \int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^t \dot h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s . \tag{9.73}\]
Proof

We have to show that for \(t_0 = 0\) the integral \(u(t) = \int_0^t h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\) solves the equation with initial values zero. We differentiate it twice with lemma 9.77, use \(h(0) = 0\), \(m\,\dot h(0) = 1\) and the equation for \(h\), and uniqueness is given by theorem 9.36. At the end we shift the time.

1. The function \(h\) on all real numbers.

  1. By definition 9.74 and the argument after it, \(h\) is differentiable as many times as we like on the whole axis (sums and products of the exponential function, sine, cosine or hyperbolic functions and a polynomial: theorem 9.13, point 2, theorem 8.12, lemma 1.81), so \(h\), \(\dot h\) and \(\ddot h\) are continuous (corollary 1.64). At \(u = 0\) we have \(h(0) = 0\) and \(\dot h(0) = 1/m\).
  2. By definition 9.74, \(m\,\ddot h + c\,\dot h + k\,h = 0\) for every real \(u\).

2. The integral solves the equation (start time \(t_0 = 0\)).

  1. The kernels \(g(t, s) = h(t - s)\) and \(g_1(t, s) = \dot h(t - s)\) are continuous on \([0, T]^2\). For every \(s\) they are differentiable in \(t\) (chain rule, lemma 8.29, point 1, for the shift \(t \mapsto t - s\) with derivative \(1\)) with derivatives \(\partial g/\partial t = \dot h(t - s)\) and \(\partial g_1/\partial t = \ddot h(t - s)\), which are continuous by step 1. Lemma 9.77 holds for both kernels.
  2. By point 1 of the lemma \(u\) is continuous. By point 2, at every point \(t\) that is not a break point of the force, \(u\) is differentiable and, since \(g(t, t) = h(0) = 0\),
    \[\begin{aligned} u'(t) &= h(0)\,Q(t) + \int_0^t \dot h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = u_1(t) , \\ u_1(t) &= \int_0^t \dot h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s . \end{aligned}\]
  3. By point 1 of the lemma, applied to \(g_1\), \(u_1\) is continuous. The function \(u\) is continuous and at every point that is not a break point differentiable with derivative \(u_1\), so it is piecewise continuously differentiable (definition 6.11). By lemma 6.12, \(u(t) = u(0) + \int_0^t u_1(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^t u_1(x)\,\mathrm{d}x\), since \(u(0) = 0\). The function \(u_1\) is continuous, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus (theorem 3.40, point 2) \(u\) is differentiable at every point of \([0, T]\) with derivative \(u' = u_1\). Therefore \(u'\) is continuous and \(u'(0) = u_1(0) = 0\).
  4. By point 2 of the lemma, applied to \(g_1\), at every point \(t\) that is not a break point \(u'\) is differentiable and, since \(\dot h(0) = 1/m\) by step 1,
    \[u''(t) = \dot h(0)\,Q(t) + \int_0^t \ddot h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = \frac{1}{m}\,Q(t) + \int_0^t \ddot h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s .\]
  5. By step 2, \(\ddot h = -(c\,\dot h + k\,h)/m\) everywhere, so by linearity of the integral (lemma 6.10, point 2) the integral in step 6 equals \(-(c\,u_1(t) + k\,u(t))/m\). Hence at every point that is not a break point
    \[m\,u'' + c\,u' + k\,u = Q(t) .\]
    On every open piece \((s_{\mathrm{i}}, s_{\mathrm{i}+1})\) on which \(Q = Q_{\mathrm{i}}\), \(u''\) equals the function \((Q_{\mathrm{i}} - c\,u_1 - k\,u)/m\), which is continuous on the closed piece. Therefore \(u'\) is piecewise continuously differentiable. The function \(u\) is thus a solution in the sense above, with \(u(0) = 0\) and \(u'(0) = 0\).
  6. The function \(q_{\mathrm{pr}}\) is a solution of the free equation. The function \(q = q_{\mathrm{pr}} + u\) is therefore a solution of the equation with force \(Q\) (lemma 9.6, applied at every point that is not a break point, since its proof needs only the linearity of differentiation at a point). The functions \(q\) and \(\dot q = \dot q_{\mathrm{pr}} + u_1\) are continuous, \(\dot q\) is piecewise continuously differentiable, \(q(0) = q_0\) and \(\dot q(0) = v_0\). Thus \(\dot q\) has the form (9.73).
  7. Uniqueness. Let \(\tilde q\) be another solution on \([0, T]\) with the same initial values. Both are solutions of order \(2\) of the same equation with the same piecewise continuous force, so by theorem 9.36 (a real function is a complex one with imaginary part zero) they are equal.

3. Start time \(t_0\).

  1. Let \(T' = T - t_0\), \(\tilde Q(\sigma) = Q(t_0 + \sigma)\) and \(\tilde q(\sigma) = q(t_0 + \sigma)\) for \(\sigma \in [0, T']\). The function \(\tilde Q\) is piecewise continuous with break points shifted by \(t_0\). By the chain rule (lemma 8.29, point 1, the shift \(\sigma \mapsto t_0 + \sigma\) has derivative \(1\), the functions \(q\) and \(\dot q\) are continuously differentiable on open pieces) \(\tilde q' (\sigma) = \dot q(t_0 + \sigma)\) and \(\tilde q''(\sigma) = \ddot q(t_0 + \sigma)\) at every point that is not a break point. The coefficients are constant, so \(q\) is a solution on \([t_0, T]\) with force \(Q\) exactly when \(\tilde q\) is a solution on \([0, T']\) with force \(\tilde Q\), and the initial values agree.
  2. By lemma 9.78, point 2, with \(G(s) = h(t - s)\,Q(s)\), \(p = t_0\), \(q = t\) and \(d = t_0\) we have \(\int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^t h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s = \int_0^{t - t_0} h(t - t_0 - \sigma)\,\tilde Q(\sigma)\,\mathrm{d}\sigma\), which is the integral of the case \(t_0 = 0\) for \(\tilde Q\) at time \(t - t_0\). The free part is \(q_{\mathrm{pr}}(t) = \tilde q_{\mathrm{pr}}(t - t_0)\) with the free motion \(\tilde q_{\mathrm{pr}} = q_0\varphi_1 + v_0\varphi_2\). The case \(t_0 = 0\) for \(\tilde Q\) gives the claim, and the same for (9.73).

Source: CK (5.32)-(5.34), PDF pp. 143-144 ("Duhamel integral") and GR (2.113), PDF p. 111, for the formula. The proof by verification, uniqueness and the shift of time is not from a source, CK and GR derive the formula by adding the responses to pulses, as in the introduction of the section.

The theorem says that the motion consists of two parts: the free motion that the initial state starts, and the response from rest to the force, which is the integral \(\int_{\mathrm{t}_0}^t h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\). We call the integral the convolution integral (konvolucijski integral) or the Duhamel integral (Duhamelov integral). The proof never needed the force to "break up" into pulses. It needed only that \(h\) is a solution of free vibration with velocity \(1/m\) at time zero and that the equation is linear.

Let us check the theorem on A for the step \(Q(t) = Q_0\) for \(t \ge 0\). Then by the theorem \(q(t) = Q_0 \int_0^t h(t - s)\,\mathrm{d}s\), and by lemma 9.78, point 1, with \(G = h\) we have \(\int_0^t h(t - s)\,\mathrm{d}s = \int_0^t h(u)\,\mathrm{d}u\). At \(t = 0{,}3\) s this integral gives \(2{,}127327 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m/N, and the response to a step from theorem 9.69, \((1 - e^{-\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}} t}(\cos\omega_{\mathrm{d}} t + (\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}}/\omega_{\mathrm{d}})\sin\omega_{\mathrm{d}} t))/k\), gives the same number to \(14\) digits.

9.10.5 The graph of the convolution and the memory of the system

How do we read the value \(q(t)\) from a picture, without computing? At each \(t\) we draw \(Q(s)\) and \(h(t - s)\) as functions of the variable \(s\) (figure 9.40). The function \(s \mapsto h(t - s)\) is \(h\) reflected about a vertical line and moved so that its start, \(h(0) = 0\), lies at \(s = t\). The response to a pulse at time \(s\) has the value \(h(t - s)\) at time \(t\), so \(h(t - s)\) is a weight: how much of the pulse at time \(s\) is still in motion at time \(t\). The product \(Q(s)\,h(t - s)\) is the contribution of the force at time \(s\), and \(q(t)\) is its signed area from \(s = 0\) to \(s = t\). As \(t\) grows, the weight moves along the force like a window. In the figure there are three times, and in each of them the area of the positive (blue) parts and of the negative (grey) parts is different.

The graphical procedure is not from a source: we did not find it in the sources of this project, so we use it only as an explanation of a formula that is already proved.

The system remembers forces from the past, but not for ever. The envelope of the weight \(h(t - s)\), that is the curve \(e^{-\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}} u}/(m\omega_{\mathrm{d}})\) with \(u = t - s\) that the peaks of the vibration do not exceed, falls to one hundredth of its initial value at \(u = \ln 100/(\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}}) = 13{,}0\) s (figure 9.41, \(\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}} = 0{,}3542\) 1/s). We estimate the contribution of all forces older than \(\tau\) as follows. If \(|Q| \le Q_{\max}\), then by lemma 9.78 (point 1, the second equality in (9.71), applied on \([0, t - \tau]\) instead of on \([t - \tau, t]\)), the estimate \(|\int f| \le \int |f|\) (lemma 9.31, a real function is a complex one with imaginary part zero) and the estimate \(|\sin| \le 1\), so \(|h(u)| \le e^{-\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}} u}/(m\omega_{\mathrm{d}})\),

\[\Big| \int_0^{t - \tau} h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s \Big| \le Q_{\max} \int_\tau^t \frac{e^{-\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}} u}}{m\omega_{\mathrm{d}}}\,\mathrm{d}u \le \frac{Q_{\max}\,e^{-\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\tau}}{\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\,m\omega_{\mathrm{d}}} .\]

The last step is the integral \(\int_\tau^t e^{-au}\,\mathrm{d}u = (e^{-a\tau} - e^{-at})/a \le e^{-a\tau}/a\) with \(a = \zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\) (theorem 3.40, the derivative of the function \(-e^{-au}/a\) is \(e^{-au}\)). The static displacement under the force \(Q_{\max}\) is \(Q_{\max}/k\), so the right-hand side is the fraction \(\dfrac{\omega_{\mathrm{n}}}{\zeta\,\omega_{\mathrm{d}}}\,e^{-\zeta\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\tau}\) of the static displacement, since \(k = m\omega_{\mathrm{n}}^2\). At \(\tau = 13{,}0\) s this is \(1{,}0\), at \(\tau = 26{,}0\) s it is \(0{,}010\). The estimate uses only the absolute value of \(h\) and does not take into account that the signs of the vibration partly cancel in the integral, so it is an upper bound. Forces older than \(26\) s therefore change the displacement by no more than about one percent of the static displacement, and forces older than \(13\) s by at most one static displacement. The free motion that an initial state starts (section 9.5) has the same envelope: the system also forgets its initial state in the same time, for A it falls to one hundredth of its initial value in \(13\) s.

9.10.6 Examples

The rectangular pulse once more. A force \(Q_0 = 1\) N acts on A (\(\zeta = 0{,}01\)) from \(0\) to \(t_{\mathrm{d}} = T_{\mathrm{n}}/4 = 0{,}04435\) s and is zero afterwards. What is the response at time \(t = 0{,}3\) s? By theorem 9.79 (initial values zero) and lemma 9.78, point 1, with \(G(s) = h(t - s)\) on \([0, t_{\mathrm{d}}]\) and \(d = t\) we have

\[q(t) = \int_0^{t_{\mathrm{d}}} h(t - s)\,\mathrm{d}s = \int_{\mathrm{t} - \mathrm{t}_\mathrm{d}}^{t} h(u)\,\mathrm{d}u ,\]

which is the reflection of the interval \([0, t_{\mathrm{d}}]\) about \(t/2\). This integral is the difference \(\int_0^t h - \int_0^{t - t_{\mathrm{d}}} h\), and \(\int_0^t h(u)\,\mathrm{d}u\) is, by the above, the response to a step \(u_{\mathrm{st}}(t)\) from section 9.9. The response to the rectangular pulse is therefore \(u_{\mathrm{st}}(t) - u_{\mathrm{st}}(t - t_{\mathrm{d}})\), the difference of two steps of which the second is delayed by \(t_{\mathrm{d}}\), which is the path of section 9.9. Three computations give the same value at \(t = 0{,}3\) s: the quadrature of the integral \(\int_0^{t_{\mathrm{d}}} h(t - s)\,\mathrm{d}s\) (mpmath), the quadrature of \(\int_{\mathrm{t} - \mathrm{t}_\mathrm{d}}^t h(u)\,\mathrm{d}u\) and the difference of the step responses, all \(-8{,}191866 \cdot 10^{-6}\) m (agreement to \(14\) digits). The sign is negative because the argument \(\omega_{\mathrm{d}}(t - s)\) in the integral changes from \(9{,}054\) to \(10{,}625\) rad. The sine is positive up to \(3\pi = 9{,}425\) rad and negative after that, so most of the interval is negative. Figure 9.42 shows the response for all times.

The ramp (rampa). We load the weight on the cantilever A gradually: the force grows linearly from \(0\) to the weight \(Q_0 = 490{,}5\) N in time \(t_{\mathrm{r}}\) and then stays \(Q_0\) (CK (5.14)-(5.15), PDF p. 139). How long should the loading last so that the cantilever does not start to swing? First without damping, \(c = 0\), \(\omega = \omega_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(h(u) = \sin(\omega u)/(m\omega)\), and \(m\omega^2 = k\).

  1. For \(0 \le t \le t_{\mathrm{r}}\) we have \(Q(s) = Q_0\,s/t_{\mathrm{r}}\). By lemma 9.78, point 1, \(q(t) = \int_0^t h(u)\,Q_0\,(t - u)/t_{\mathrm{r}}\,\mathrm{d}u = \dfrac{Q_0}{m\omega\,t_{\mathrm{r}}}\int_0^t (t - u)\sin\omega u\,\mathrm{d}u\).
  2. The integrals are \(\int_0^t \sin\omega u\,\mathrm{d}u = (1 - \cos\omega t)/\omega\) and \(\int_0^t u\sin\omega u\,\mathrm{d}u = (\sin\omega t - \omega t\cos\omega t)/\omega^2\). We check the second by differentiation: the derivative of the function \((\sin\omega u - \omega u\cos\omega u)/\omega^2\) is \((\omega\cos\omega u - \omega\cos\omega u + \omega^2 u\sin\omega u)/\omega^2 = u\sin\omega u\), zero at \(u = 0\) (theorem 3.40).
  3. Hence \(q(t) = \dfrac{Q_0}{m\omega\,t_{\mathrm{r}}}\Big(\dfrac{t(1 - \cos\omega t)}{\omega} - \dfrac{\sin\omega t - \omega t\cos\omega t}{\omega^2}\Big) = \dfrac{Q_0}{k}\Big(\dfrac{t}{t_{\mathrm{r}}} - \dfrac{\sin\omega t}{\omega t_{\mathrm{r}}}\Big)\), which is CK (5.18). The derivative is \(\dot q = \dfrac{Q_0}{k t_{\mathrm{r}}}(1 - \cos\omega t) \ge 0\), so \(q\) does not decrease.
  4. Step 3 is the function \(R\) of step 1 in the proof of lemma 9.70, so the convolution gives the same as the lemma for \(0 \le t \le t_{\mathrm{r}}\). By theorem 9.79 the convolution is the only solution of the equation with this force that is at rest at \(t = 0\), so for \(t \ge t_{\mathrm{r}}\) it equals the solution of the lemma,
    \[q(t) = \frac{Q_0}{k}\Big(1 - \frac{\sin x}{x}\cos\omega\big(t - \tfrac{t_{\mathrm{r}}}{2}\big)\Big) , \qquad x = \frac{\pi t_{\mathrm{r}}}{T_{\mathrm{n}}} ,\]
    that is a vibration about the static displacement \(Q_0/k\) with the amplitude \(|\sin x|/x\) (in units of \(Q_0/k\)), as in equation (9.63) with \(\theta = x\) (CK (5.19)). By the same lemma the largest value is \(\dfrac{Q_0}{k}\Big(1 + \dfrac{|\sin x|}{x}\Big)\).

The largest displacement is therefore \(1 + |\sin x|/x\) times the static one, where \(x = \pi t_{\mathrm{r}}/T_{\mathrm{n}}\). For \(t_{\mathrm{r}} \to 0\) we have \(|\sin x|/x \to 1\) and get twice the static displacement, as for a step (section 9.9). For \(t_{\mathrm{r}} = T_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(2T_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(\dots\) we have \(\sin x = 0\) and there is no vibration, because the initial and the final bend of the force (\(\dot Q\) jumps from \(0\) to \(Q_0/t_{\mathrm{r}}\) and back) start two free vibrations of equal size with opposite signs and shifted by a whole period, which add in the formula to \(\sin\omega(t - t_{\mathrm{r}}) - \sin\omega t = 0\). The static displacement of A is \(Q_0/k = 7{,}8205\) mm. The stress at the root under the weight is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = -M\,y/I\) (chapter 5, cantilever clamped at \(x = 0\) with a downward force at the free end: \(M = -Q_0 L = -490{,}5\) N m with \(L = 1\) m). At the upper edge of the cross-section, \(y = 20\) mm (half the height), and \(I = 106\,667\) mm\(^4\) we have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = 490{,}5\ \text{N m} \cdot 0{,}020\ \text{m}/(1{,}06667 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^4) = 91{,}97\) MPa, tension. The results are

\(t_{\mathrm{r}}/T_{\mathrm{n}}\) \(0{,}5\) \(1\) \(1{,}5\) \(5\)
\(1 + \lvert\sin x\rvert/x\) \(1{,}6366\) \(1{,}0000\) \(1{,}2122\) \(1{,}0000\)
largest displacement, \(\zeta = 0\) (mm) \(12{,}80\) \(7{,}82\) \(9{,}48\) \(7{,}82\)
largest stress at the root (MPa) \(150{,}5\) \(91{,}97\) \(111{,}5\) \(91{,}97\)
largest displacement, \(\zeta = 0{,}01\) (mm) \(12{,}645\) \(7{,}895\) \(9{,}381\) \(7{,}887\)

The stress is proportional to the displacement of the end (linear elasticity), so at \(t_{\mathrm{r}} = T_{\mathrm{n}}/2\) the largest stress is \(91{,}97 \cdot 1{,}6366 = 150{,}5\) MPa, below the yield limit (meja tečenja) \(220\) MPa, and for a step (\(t_{\mathrm{r}} = 0\)) \(183{,}9\) MPa. The last row is NumPy, convolution with \(4 \cdot 10^4\) points. Damping changes the numbers. At \(t_{\mathrm{r}} = T_{\mathrm{n}}\) there is no longer a zero, because the vibration started at the beginning decayed until \(t_{\mathrm{r}}\) by the factor \(e^{-2\pi\zeta} = 0{,}939\) and the subtraction is not complete, the remainder is \(0{,}061\,/\,(2\pi) = 0{,}97\) % of the static displacement, which agrees with \(7{,}895/7{,}8205 = 1{,}0095\). At \(t_{\mathrm{r}} = 5T_{\mathrm{n}}\) the factor is \(e^{-10\pi\zeta} = 0{,}730\) and the remainder \(0{,}86\) %, the computation gives \(0{,}84\) %. A ramp longer than a few periods therefore acts almost as a static load, as CK writes (PDF pp. 139-140), but the remainder depends on \(\zeta\).

A force known by samples. We know the force on A only as values that a force gauge measured at equal time steps. Take the same pulse \(Q(s) = 20\ \text{N}\,\sin(\pi s/t_{\mathrm{p}})\) with \(t_{\mathrm{p}} = T_{\mathrm{n}}/2\), measured with \(n = 8\) steps, that is with \(9\) samples \(Q_{\mathrm{j}}\) at times \(s_{\mathrm{j}} = j\,t_{\mathrm{p}}/8\) for \(j = 0, \dots, 8\): \(0\), \(7{,}654\), \(14{,}142\), \(18{,}478\), \(20\), \(18{,}478\), \(14{,}142\), \(7{,}654\) and \(0\) N. We do not use a formula for \(Q(s)\), we have only these values, and at the sample times we can compute \(f_{\mathrm{j}} = h(t - s_{\mathrm{j}})\,Q_{\mathrm{j}}\). We replace the integral by the trapezoidal rule (trapezna vsota): on each step \(\Delta s\) we take the area of a trapezoid, that is the average of the values of the integrand \(f_{\mathrm{j}} = h(t - s_{\mathrm{j}})\,Q_{\mathrm{j}}\) at the edges times the step, which altogether gives \(\Delta s\,(f_0/2 + f_1 + \dots + f_{\mathrm{n}-1} + f_{\mathrm{n}}/2)\). At \(t = 0{,}3\) s, \(n = 4\), \(8\) (the \(9\) samples above) and \(16\) steps give \(q = 0{,}167469\), \(0{,}167817\) and \(0{,}167900\) mm, and the exact integral is \(0{,}167928\) mm. The errors are \(-0{,}273\) %, \(-0{,}0661\) % and \(-0{,}0164\) %. When the step is halved, the error decreases by about a factor of \(4\) (\(4{,}13\) and \(4{,}03\)), as we expect for the trapezoidal rule, whose error is proportional to the square of the step (not proved here). Since the end values at \(j = 0\) and \(j = n\) are zero, the halves of the end terms drop out and the trapezoidal sum is just \(\Delta s\,\sum_{\mathrm{j}} f_{\mathrm{j}}\). This is why the convolution integral is used for measured inputs: the sum needs only the measured values of the force and the computable values of \(h\), no formula for \(Q(s)\).

9.10.7 A pulse of arbitrarily short duration

Section 9.9 showed that a rectangular pulse without damping of length \(\varepsilon\) and impulse \(I\) acts as \(I\,h(t)\) with an error of amplitude and a delay. What about a pulse of any shape? The convolution gives the same estimate for every shape.

Corollary 9.80 A short pulse of any shape acts as its impulse (poljubno kratek sunek deluje kot impulz)

Let \(h\) be the impulse response of a system with \(m, k > 0\) and \(c \ge 0\) (definition 9.74) and \(Q\) a piecewise continuous function on \([0, T]\) that is zero for \(s > \varepsilon\), \(0 < \varepsilon < T\), so a pulse of length \(\varepsilon\) (section 9.9). Let \(I = \int_0^\varepsilon Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\) be its impulse (definition 9.71), \(\bar I = \int_0^\varepsilon |Q(s)|\,\mathrm{d}s\) and \(M = \max_{0 \le \mathrm{u} \le \mathrm{T}} |\dot h(u)|\), which exists by theorem 1.73 because \(\dot h\) is continuous. For the response \(q\) of the system from rest we have, for every \(t\) with \(\varepsilon \le t \le T\),

\[|q(t) - I\,h(t)| \le \varepsilon\,\bar I\,M .\]
Proof

We have to show that for \(t \ge \varepsilon\) the convolution integral and \(I\,h(t)\) differ by at most \(\varepsilon\,\bar I\,M\). We write the difference as one integral and estimate it with the mean value theorem.

  1. By theorem 9.79 with \(t_0 = 0\) and \(q_0 = v_0 = 0\) we have \(q(t) = \int_0^t h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\). Since \(Q = 0\) for \(s > \varepsilon\) and \(t \ge \varepsilon\), \(q(t) = \int_0^\varepsilon h(t - s)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  2. By linearity \(I\,h(t) = \int_0^\varepsilon h(t)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\), so \(q(t) - I\,h(t) = \int_0^\varepsilon \big(h(t - s) - h(t)\big)\,Q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s\).
  3. For \(0 < s \le \varepsilon \le t\) the function \(h\) is continuously differentiable on \([t - s, t] \subset [0, T]\), so by the mean value theorem (theorem 1.84) there is \(\xi \in (t - s, t)\) with \(h(t) - h(t - s) = \dot h(\xi)\,s\). Hence \(|h(t - s) - h(t)| \le M\,s \le M\,\varepsilon\), also at \(s = 0\).
  4. A real function is a complex one with imaginary part zero, so the estimate \(|\int f| \le \int |f|\) (lemma 9.31) holds for the piecewise continuous function \(s \mapsto (h(t - s) - h(t))\,Q(s)\). By step 3 this is in absolute value at most \(M\,\varepsilon\,|Q(s)|\), the integral preserves inequality (lemma 6.10, point 3), so \(|q(t) - I\,h(t)| \le \int_0^\varepsilon M\,\varepsilon\,|Q(s)|\,\mathrm{d}s = \varepsilon\,\bar I\,M\).

Source: The proof is not from a source. CK (PDF p. 143) says: "an excitation can be considered to be an impulse if \(t_{\mathrm{d}} \ll T_{\mathrm{n}}\)", without an estimate.

The corollary completes the idea of section 9.9: the error is proportional to the length of the pulse \(\varepsilon\), for every shape of the force. We check on A. Let \(\varepsilon = T_{\mathrm{n}}/10 = 0{,}01774\) s, \(I = 5\) N s (a rectangular pulse \(Q_0 = I/\varepsilon = 281{,}8\) N), \(\bar I = 5\) N s, and \(M = 1/m = 0{,}02\) 1/kg (the largest value of \(|\dot h|\) is \(\dot h(0) = 1/m\), NumPy on \([0, 1]\) s, later the envelope falls below this value). The estimate is \(\varepsilon\,\bar I\,M = 1{,}774\) mm. The amplitude of the motion \(I\,h\) is \(I/(m\omega_{\mathrm{d}}) = 2{,}824\) mm, so the estimate is \(62{,}8\) % of the amplitude. The actual largest deviation \(|q - I\,h|\) for \(t \ge \varepsilon\) is \(0{,}850\) mm, \(30{,}1\) % of the amplitude. The estimate is twice too high because we bound \(h(t - s) - h(t)\) by the time \(\varepsilon\), while the real delay of the pulse is its midpoint, \(\varepsilon/2\), which is a shift of \(\omega_{\mathrm{n}}\varepsilon/2 = 0{,}314\) rad and at most \(2\sin(0{,}157) = 31\) % of the amplitude, as in section 9.9. For \(\varepsilon = T_{\mathrm{n}}/100\) the estimate is \(0{,}1774\) mm, \(6{,}3\) % of the amplitude. The estimate is rough, but it says the same as the exact computation: for every shape of a shorter pulse the error is proportional to the length.

9.10.8 Names and continuation

Other books write a pulse as \(Q(t) = I\,\delta(t - s)\) with the Dirac delta (Diracova delta) and call \(h\) the response to the delta. KREYSZIG (§6.4, PDF p. 252) says that the delta "is not a function in the ordinary sense as used in calculus", and this book does not use it: we treated the pulse with the impulse response, which is an ordinary function, and with corollary 9.80. The convolution integral is the content of the convolution theorem (konvolucijski izrek) on integral transforms, by which the transform of a convolution is the product of the transforms (KREYSZIG §6.5, PDF p. 258). We do not use the Laplace transform in the book.

With one integral the section told what system A does under a force of any shape, known by a formula or by samples. For the periodic force later in the chapter the convolution, written by lemma 9.78 as \(\int_0^\infty h(u)\,Q(t - u)\,\mathrm{d}u\), will give the response to a force that has been acting since for ever.
